posts.title: I killed a week-long experiment because the thing I was testing had already read the answers
posts.excerpt: I spent about a week building a controlled experiment to find out whether my own setup is worth anything, and then I killed it. The setup is the pile of stuff I have bolted onto Claude Code over the last few months. A vault of notes, a stack of skills, a router file that tells th
posts.text:
I spent about a week building a controlled experiment to find out whether my own
setup is worth anything, and then I killed it. The setup is the pile of stuff I have
bolted onto Claude Code over the last few months. A vault of notes, a stack of
skills, a router file that tells the agent which skill to grab, a context layer, and
a memory system that carries what I learned in one repo into every other repo. It
all feels useful. Feels. Nobody had measured it, me least of all.

So: ablation study. Same tasks under the full stack, then again with one piece
pulled out at a time, and whatever hurts when you pull it is the piece doing work.
167 reps per cell. 8,183 runs. Pre-registered and frozen before a single run so I
could not drift the goalposts once numbers started landing, which I would have.

Zero of those runs happened.

The gate that ate it

Before a task's first scored run there is a check that greps every memory store on
the machine for that task's distinctive strings. If the answer is already sitting
somewhere an agent can retrieve, I am not measuring reasoning, I am measuring
lookup. Any hit burns the task. Fail-closed, no override switch, because the only
person who would ever reach for the override is me at 1am wanting the number.

All seven tasks burned. Nothing scored, ever.

The first cause is embarrassing and boring. I had sub-agents write the tasks on this
machine, so every task matched its own authoring transcript. Transcripts are memory.
I knew that. I had written it down in the same repo a week earlier, in a file about
this exact hazard. Moved the authoring off the machine, re-scanned, four of seven
came back clean.

Then the second cause.

The memory system had already filed it

My cross-project memory had consolidated pieces of the experiment into records
belonging to two unrelated projects. Spec revisions, task file paths, and in one case
the literal edit that introduced a task's answer string, sitting in a record filed
under a project that has nothing to do with any of this.

Nothing read the experiment's repo. There was no crawl to block, no directory to add
to an ignore list, no leak in the sense of something escaping through a hole. The
content showed up pre-formed, already summarized, filed while I worked. The memory
system was doing the job I built it for. The job is to notice what I am doing and
make it available later, in every other project. It did that. It is good at it.

And two of the conditions under test are memory and vault access. That is what kills
it. The leak is not even across arms. The full-stack arm can retrieve the leaked
answer, the stripped-down arm cannot reach it, so some slice of whatever gap I
measured is my own experiment handed back to me, and I would have read that slice as
the harness earning its keep. Which is the claim. That is the whole thing I sat down
to test.

If you run agent memory across projects and you also want to evaluate those agents on
anything, this is sitting there waiting for you. Your eval material is material. It
gets consolidated like everything else. The isolation you think you have is
repo-shaped, memory ignores repo shape, that is the product.

The bit I liked less

Writing up the kill I reread my own pre-registration and found something worse than
the leak, which is a sentence I did not enjoy typing.

Three tasks. One per task shape. 8,183 runs across three tasks. All that repetition
buys precision and precision is not generality, so I would have finished with a very
tight measurement of three specific tasks and no standing to say a word about a
fourth. The limitation is written into the pre-registration. In my own words. I read
it during review and approved it, because the run count looked serious and I wanted
to start.

So the clean version of this experiment was going to hand me a number I could not
use. I got saved from that by a grep.

What I am doing instead

Bake-off on real tickets out of live repos. Full stack against bare, same ticket,
judged blind. Contamination stops mattering once the tasks are work I wanted done
anyway, and if the harness wins partly by retrieving something it stashed earlier,
fine, that is the harness doing its job. Looser instrument. Worse paper. Measures a
thing I care about.

The actual mistake was sequencing. I built the apparatus first, all of it,
pre-registration and frozen spec and an adversarial review panel and contamination
scanning and isolation proofs, and the apparatus is good. I built it before checking
whether the thing I wanted to measure was measurable on this machine, with this
memory running, on tasks of this kind. That check is an afternoon. It goes first, and
I knew that, and I did it in the other order anyway.

posts.title: I asked two AI models to destroy my work. They disagreed about how.
posts.excerpt: For the last few weeks I have been designing a piece of software, and before any decision gets locked I hand the write-up to two AI models and ask them to break it. Kimi and Codex. Same brief, sent in parallel. Neither can see the other's response, and neither remembers the last
posts.text:
For the last few weeks I have been designing a piece of software, and before any
decision gets locked I hand the write-up to two AI models and ask them to break
it. Kimi and Codex. Same brief, sent in parallel. Neither can see the other's
response, and neither remembers the last round.

The setup was meant to catch my mistakes, which it does. It also taught me
something about reviewing that I did not go looking for.

Same brief, different reviewers

The important detail first, because it is what makes the rest meaningful: both
models get the identical file. Same bytes. Same opening line telling them they
are an adversarial reviewer and should default to skepticism. Neither one is
told to be harsher than the other.

Here is what came back on the same document, on the same day.

Kimi 
 Codex 

words 
 2,706 
 1,915 

numeric claims 
 15 
 6 

bullet points 
 31 
 88 

average sentence length 
 31.8 words 
 31.9 words 

Average sentence length matches to a tenth of a word, so neither is padding.
What differs is where they go.

Kimi is the empiricist. It re-ran my measurement script, without being asked to,
and compared its own output against the figures I had published. That is how it
found the error: I had been counting text written by AI subagents as though a
human had typed it. I published 10.6 percent as 14.4 percent. It then quoted my
own script's documentation back at me, which had warned against exactly that
mistake. I had written the warning and then ignored it.

Codex is the structuralist. It went looking for my experiments folder before
reading anything, and attacked the shape of my argument rather than its
arithmetic. Its finding was that my headline metric multiplied five rates
measured over four different populations. The arithmetic was correct. The number
meant nothing.

Then both of them opened with the same two objections. They run in parallel,
memoryless, unable to coordinate. That agreement carried more weight than either
review alone, and it convinced me to rebuild the document rather than patch it.

The two days I spent trying to make one of them fair

Kimi has a habit that took me a while to understand. It never stops. Every round
produces fresh criticism, all of it individually defensible, and I could keep
revising forever without ever arriving at "this is finished."

For a while I read that as temperament, so I tried to fix it the way everyone
tries to fix it. I rewrote the instructions.

I ran this properly, over three days in July, with a sealed holdout set and a
pre-registered decision rule. The question was narrow: can any wording make this
model a useful pass-or-fail gate on a specification? I gave it more context, then
less. I told it to be harsher. I told it to be gentler. I moved the stated
failure rate up and down, and the stated cost of missing something.

The answer was no, and the shape of the no is the part worth having.

It flagged 82 percent of specifications when 35 percent of them were actually
bad. A rubber stamp that read nothing and approved everything scored better than
every prompt I wrote. On obviously good specs and obviously terrible ones it was
perfect. On real ones it was a coin flip.

Every tone lever moved the flag rate and none of them improved the accuracy.
Tilting it toward flagging produced nine false alarms and zero real catches. Its
sense of what looks risky turns out to be uncorrelated with what is actually
broken. This is the finding I keep coming back to, because "just tell it to be
more critical" is the first thing anyone reaches for and it is worse than
useless. It produces more noise that feels like more rigour.

More instruction made it monotonically worse. Every added distinction raised its
flagging without adding a single new catch. One rewrite collapsed it into
approving everything.

My best configuration scored 44 out of 50 on the data I tuned it against, then
caught zero of three real failures on the sealed holdout. It had memorised the
phrasing of the examples I let it see rather than learning anything.

I filed the whole thing as a failed experiment and moved on.

It was not a failed experiment

Three days later I was writing up the review process and realised the null result
was the load-bearing part.

The model that loses to a rubber stamp on pass-or-fail is the same model that
re-ran my script and caught a real error in my published numbers. Both of those
are true at once, and I had been treating them as one purchase.

Finding things and judging things are separate skills, and this reviewer has one
of them.

So the process I ended up with never asks a model for a verdict. It asks for
findings, and every finding has to cite a line, a number, or a specific
inference. Anything that cannot point at something is advisory by default.
Findings get sorted into fatal, material, and advisory, and only fatal blocks
acceptance.

Review stops when a round produces nothing fatal, with a hard cap of three
rounds. And the rule that actually made it terminate: later rounds may only check
whether earlier findings were resolved. They may not open new ground. New ground
becomes a separate task.

Without that last rule, every round legitimately discovers something new, because
any document is infinitely criticisable, and the sequence never ends. With it,
the loop is bounded by the first round's findings, which is a finite list. The
reviewer stopped being the thing that decides when I am done, which was the real
problem all along. Before, that decision was made by whatever hour I ran out of
patience.

A postscript about losing my own work

While writing this I could not find the three-day experiment I just described. It
was on my own laptop, committed to git, in a folder two directories from where I
was working, finished the previous week.

I searched for "prompt engineering." I searched for "tone" across 3,483
conversation transcripts. I ran a full content search across every project folder
for "harsh," "be kind," and half a dozen similar phrases. All of it came back
empty, or came back with results about email etiquette.

The document that answered the question was sitting right there. It just never
uses those words. It says propensity levers, base rate, cost asymmetry, flag
rate. I had named the work for what it measured, and I went looking for it using
the words I would have described it with months later. Both descriptions are
correct. They share no vocabulary.

What eventually found it was listing my folders by date and reading the names.

Nothing was lost, corrupted, or missing. Storage was perfect. Retrieval failed
completely, on the gap between how I filed something and how I later asked for
it. That is a more honest argument for better search than any benchmark I could
have designed, and I got it by accident, from failing at it.

Two caveats, because they matter

The prompt was identical for both models. The surrounding software was not: each
runs through its own command line tool with its own defaults. The comparison is
controlled on instructions and imperfectly controlled on environment, and a
cleaner version of this would hold both fixed.

The calibration result is about one model at one task, gating specifications. It
is not a claim about that model generally, and it is certainly not a claim about
the others. What generalises is the method: measure your reviewer against a
baseline that does nothing before you trust its verdicts, because a reviewer that
flags most things can look rigorous while carrying no information at all.
